detailed_rationale:
WeWork India Management Ltd is the exclusive Indian licensee of the WeWork brand, majority-owned by Bengaluru's Embassy Group. As of mid-2025 it operated 68 centres across eight Tier-1 cities with roughly 1.14 lakh desks over 7.67 million sq ft, and FY26 revenue grew 25% YoY to about Rs 2,440 crore (3-year CAGR ~23%). Operating margins are strong (Q1 FY27 operating margin ~64%) because the model is largely fixed-cost real-estate arbitrage on long leases, but the bottom line is far more volatile than the operating line suggests: a healthy Rs 65.87 crore net profit in Q4 FY26 flipped to a small Rs 4.06 crore net loss in Q1 FY27 (Jun 2026) despite a similar operating margin, most likely from lease-accounting/interest-timing effects under Ind AS 116 rather than any change in underlying demand.

The balance sheet is the part of the story that worries me more than the P&L. Borrowings jumped from about Rs 310 crore to Rs 5,550 crore in a single year to fund new centre build-outs, book value per share is a thin Rs 22 against a ~Rs 744 share price (33.6x price-to-book), and the stock trades around 116x trailing earnings. Interest coverage is already flagged as weak, and with debt roughly 18x higher than a year ago, financing costs will keep climbing against a membership-revenue base that is itself sensitive to office-occupancy cycles. Promoter (Embassy-linked) holding has been drifting down (49.8% to 48.3% in one quarter) with about 35% of that stake pledged, and the company pays no dividend despite reporting profits.

Reverse-DCF: at ~116x earnings and ~34x book, the market is pricing durable double-digit desk growth plus stable-to-improving margins for several years, layered on top of a debt-funded expansion model whose downside case (an occupancy wobble or a rate shock hitting the now much larger interest bill) is not small given the leverage added in just the last twelve months. The quant read (quality_score ~97.9 but value_score only ~26.6, i.e. 'expensive') captures this precisely: good current profitability, poor price for the risk now sitting on the balance sheet.
recommendation_rationale: Genuine 23-25% revenue growth and high operating margins are real, but they are already more than priced in at ~116x earnings and ~34x book, and the last twelve months added a large slug of new debt (~Rs 310cr to ~Rs 5,550cr) to fund that growth. A name this leveraged, this richly priced, and with quarterly net profit swinging from a solid gain to a loss on a similar operating margin is not a comfortable hold through an occupancy or rate shock. Sell, consistent with the quant score.
summary: WeWork India runs profitable, fast-growing co-working centres, but the stock trades at a very rich level (around 116x earnings and 34x book value) after borrowings rose sharply, from about Rs 310 crore to Rs 5,550 crore, to fund expansion. Quarterly profit has also swung from a healthy gain to a small loss on similar underlying operations, and promoters have pledged over a third of their stake. The growth story is real, but the price and the new leverage leave little room for error, so we rate this a Sell.
positive_para: Desk demand is genuine and growing: FY26 revenue rose 25% YoY on a 23% three-year CAGR, operating margins are a very high ~64%, and the company is the sole India licensee of a recognised global brand backed by a well-capitalised local promoter group (Embassy) with the balance-sheet access to keep funding expansion. Reported ROE of roughly 32% (helped by a thin equity base) and combined FII+DII ownership near 45% show real institutional acceptance of the growth story.
negative_para: The bear case sits in the balance sheet and the price, not the demand. Debt grew more than 17x in a year to fund new centres, book value per share is a mere Rs 22 against a ~Rs 744 quote, and interest coverage is already flagged weak even before that new debt has fully seasoned. Net profit swung from about +Rs 66cr to -Rs 4cr quarter over quarter despite a similar operating margin, pointing to real earnings volatility below the operating line that a ~116x P/E does not appear to price in. Add a 35%-pledged promoter stake and a zero-dividend policy despite reported profits, and the risk-reward at this price is poor even if the desk-growth story continues.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At roughly 116x trailing earnings and 34x book, the market has to be pricing several more years of 20%+ desk growth with stable-to-improving margins and no further leverage-driven earnings shocks. Given borrowings rose more than 17x in a single year and quarterly profit already swung to a loss on a similar operating margin, I judge the multiple rich versus what a debt-funded, occupancy-cyclical leasing business can reliably deliver -- this is priced for a cleaner story than the balance sheet currently supports.
